title: AsyncSequence, AsyncStream, Combine & Observation
scopeHtml: Scope: AsyncSequence/AsyncStream, Combine publishers, Observation framework, bridging to Kotlin Flow mental model, NotificationCenter, KVO.

notes.title: Baseline and the observation toolbox
notes.html:
Android equivalent. In Android you stream values with Flow/StateFlow/SharedFlow, bridge callbacks with callbackFlow, and observe UI state with collectAsStateWithLifecycle. In iOS there is no single type: you pick from AsyncSequence/AsyncStream (modern), Combine (older reactive framework), the Observation framework (@Observable, for UI state), and the old toolbox (NotificationCenter, KVO, delegates, target-action).

Baseline for this track. Swift 6 language mode, Xcode 16+, iOS 17/18 minimum, SwiftUI-first. Modern: AsyncSequence, AsyncStream, @Observable. Legacy "you will meet this in old codebases": Combine, ObservableObject/@Published, KVO, delegates.

 Question                              Reach for
 ------------------------------------  -----------------------------------
 One value later                       async/await
 Stream of values, new code            AsyncStream / AsyncSequence
 UI state a view reads                 @Observable (Observation)
 Complex operators (debounce, merge)   Combine (existing) or swift-async-algorithms
 System broadcast (keyboard, locale)   NotificationCenter (has async API)
 Property of an ObjC/UIKit object      KVO (observe) 
 One-to-one callback                   Delegate / closure
Android iOS
Flow<T> AsyncSequence / AsyncStream<T>
callbackFlow { awaitClose } AsyncStream { continuation in ... onTermination }
StateFlow @Observable property (plus CurrentValueSubject in Combine)
SharedFlow PassthroughSubject (Combine) or AsyncChannel (swift-async-algorithms)
debounce, combine, merge Combine operators or swift-async-algorithms
BroadcastReceiver NotificationCenter
LiveData observer @Published / @Observable

Analogy. These are different delivery services: a courier (async), a conveyor belt (AsyncSequence), a notice board (Observation), and a postal system with sorting rules (Combine).

Common interview traps.

  • Answering "Combine" for every reactive question in a 2025 interview. Say AsyncSequence and @Observable first, Combine as legacy.
  • Equating StateFlow with Published; StateFlow is conflated and always has a value, Published emits on every willSet.

notes.title: AsyncSequence and for await
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Flow<T> with collect { } inside a coroutine. In Swift, a stream of values is any type conforming to AsyncSequence, consumed with for await.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
for await line in url.lines {            // URL.AsyncBytes lines
    print(line)
}

// Throwing sequence
for try await event in eventStream {
    handle(event)
}
flow.collect { line ->
    println(line)
}

// Throwing flow: exception propagates out of collect
try { flow.collect { handle(it) } } catch (e: Exception) { }

Mechanism. AsyncSequence has makeAsyncIterator(), and the iterator has mutating func next() async throws -> Element?. for await calls next() repeatedly, suspending between elements, until it returns nil (finished) or throws. The loop body runs in the caller's isolation, so a for await inside a @MainActor function runs its body on main. Breaking out of the loop or cancelling the surrounding Task stops iteration and tears down the producer.

Built-in sequences.

  • URL.lines, URLSession.bytes(from:) (stream lines of a response, e.g. server-sent events).
  • NotificationCenter.notifications(named:) (iOS 15+).
  • FileHandle.bytes.
  • Observations (a stream of @Observable changes) is new in Swift 6.2/iOS 26: verify.

Operators. The standard library gives map, filter, prefix, reduce, contains, first(where:) on AsyncSequence, but not debounce, merge, combineLatest. Those live in the Apple package swift-async-algorithms (AsyncAlgorithms): debounce, throttle, merge, combineLatest, zip, chunked, AsyncChannel.

Differences from Flow.

  • Flows are cold and re-run per collector. A single AsyncStream is usually single-consumer: two for await loops split the elements between them rather than each getting all. Fan-out needs a broadcaster you write or AsyncChannel/a Combine subject.
  • No built-in flowOn; isolation is decided by where you iterate and where the producer runs.
  • No stateIn/shareIn.

Real examples. SSE parsing for ChatGPT-style streaming UIs (URLSession.bytes), Apple's CLLocationUpdate.liveUpdates() (iOS 17) and CLMonitor events are async sequences, as are StoreKit Transaction.updates and HKObserverQuery wrappers.

Analogy. A conveyor belt at sushi restaurant: you pick plates as they arrive; if you leave, the belt stops serving you.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming two consumers of one AsyncStream both receive every element.
  • Forgetting for await blocks the rest of the function; to run several sequences concurrently use child tasks (async let / TaskGroup).
  • Thinking for await loops end by themselves for infinite streams; they end on cancellation.

notes.title: AsyncStream: bridging callbacks (callbackFlow)
notes.html:
Android equivalent. callbackFlow { trySend(x); awaitClose { unregister() } }. Swift: AsyncStream (non-throwing) and AsyncThrowingStream.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
func locationUpdates(manager: CLLocationManager) -> AsyncStream<CLLocation> {
    AsyncStream { continuation in
        let delegate = LocationDelegate { location in
            continuation.yield(location)
        }
        manager.delegate = delegate
        manager.startUpdatingLocation()

        continuation.onTermination = { _ in
            manager.stopUpdatingLocation()
            withExtendedLifetime(delegate) {}   // keep delegate alive until here
        }
    }
}

// Consume
for await loc in locationUpdates(manager: manager) {
    updateMap(loc)
}
fun locationUpdates(client: FusedLocationProviderClient): Flow<Location> = callbackFlow {
    val cb = object : LocationCallback() {
        override fun onLocationResult(r: LocationResult) {
            r.lastLocation?.let { trySend(it) }
        }
    }
    client.requestLocationUpdates(request, cb, Looper.getMainLooper())
    awaitClose { client.removeLocationUpdates(cb) }
}

Mechanism. AsyncStream(Element.self, bufferingPolicy:) { continuation in ... } creates a stream with a buffer. The closure receives a Continuation (a Sendable struct) that you keep and call yield(_:) on from any thread, and finish() when done. onTermination fires when the consumer cancels, breaks, or the stream finishes: put your unregister code there.

Buffering policy (backpressure). Producers cannot be suspended by yield: it returns immediately, so the buffer policy decides what to drop.

Policy Behaviour Kotlin analogue
.unbounded (default) Keep everything; memory grows if consumer is slow Channel.UNLIMITED
.bufferingNewest(n) Keep the last n, drop older conflate() / DROP_OLDEST
.bufferingOldest(n) Keep first n, drop newer DROP_LATEST

Choose .bufferingNewest(1) for sensor data or "latest state" streams. An unbounded buffer from a hot source (location at 1 Hz is harmless; touch or accelerometer at 100 Hz with a slow consumer is not) leaks memory, visible in Instruments Allocations growing linearly.

makeStream. Swift 5.9 added AsyncStream.makeStream(of:bufferingPolicy:) returning (stream, continuation), convenient for storing the continuation as a property:

final class EventBus: Sendable {
    let events: AsyncStream<AppEvent>
    private let continuation: AsyncStream<AppEvent>.Continuation

    init() {
        (events, continuation) = AsyncStream.makeStream(of: AppEvent.self,
                                                        bufferingPolicy: .bufferingNewest(16))
    }
    func send(_ e: AppEvent) { continuation.yield(e) }
    deinit { continuation.finish() }
}

Errors. Use AsyncThrowingStream; call continuation.finish(throwing: error).

Real examples. Wrapping WCSession, CBCentralManager (Bluetooth), NWPathMonitor (reachability) and NotificationCenter observers into streams; Firebase iOS SDK addSnapshotListener wrapped as an AsyncThrowingStream (the SDK itself also provides async APIs, verify).

Analogy. A stream is a tap you connect to a doorbell: every ring fills a cup (buffer); if nobody drinks, the cup overflows or you pour out the old water, depending on the policy.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting onTermination, so the delegate/observer is never removed (leak and battery drain).
  • Calling continuation.finish() never; consumer for await hangs forever.
  • Using .unbounded for high-frequency sources.
  • Assuming yield suspends like Channel.send. It doesn't (no backpressure on producer).

notes.title: Combine: publishers, operators, subscribers
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Roughly RxJava (Observable, subscribe, CompositeDisposable) rather than Flow. You will meet Combine in old codebases and in Apple APIs that still return publishers (for example URLSession.dataTaskPublisher, NotificationCenter.publisher, Timer.publish, @Published).

The three roles.

  • Publisher: declares Output and Failure types and emits values over time.
  • Subscriber: receives values, requests demand (sink, assign).
  • Subscription: the live connection, controlling demand and cancellation.
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
import Combine

final class SearchViewModel: ObservableObject {      // legacy form
    @Published var query = ""
    @Published private(set) var results: [Item] = []
    private var cancellables = Set<AnyCancellable>()

    init(api: SearchAPI) {
        $query
            .debounce(for: .milliseconds(300), scheduler: DispatchQueue.main)
            .removeDuplicates()
            .filter { !$0.isEmpty }
            .map { q in api.searchPublisher(q).catch { _ in Just([]) } }
            .switchToLatest()
            .receive(on: DispatchQueue.main)
            .assign(to: &$results)
    }
}
class SearchViewModel(api: SearchApi) : ViewModel() {
    val query = MutableStateFlow("")
    val results: StateFlow<List<Item>> = query
        .debounce(300)
        .distinctUntilChanged()
        .filter { it.isNotEmpty() }
        .flatMapLatest { q -> flow { emit(api.search(q)) }.catch { emit(emptyList()) } }
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5000), emptyList())
}

Operator map.

Kotlin Flow Combine
map, filter map, filter
debounce debounce(for:scheduler:)
distinctUntilChanged removeDuplicates
flatMapLatest map + switchToLatest()
combine(a, b) Publishers.CombineLatest(a, b)
merge merge(with:)
catch catch, replaceError(with:)
onEach handleEvents
flowOn subscribe(on:), receive(on:)
stateIn share() / CurrentValueSubject

Subjects. PassthroughSubject (no stored value, SharedFlow-like) and CurrentValueSubject (holds a value, StateFlow-like, readable with .value).

AnyCancellable. sink returns an AnyCancellable; when it is deallocated the subscription cancels. Store in Set<AnyCancellable> on the owner, or the stream dies immediately. Typical bug: calling .sink without storing the result and getting no values.

Schedulers. receive(on: DispatchQueue.main) hops downstream to main; subscribe(on:) places the upstream work. RunLoop.main and DispatchQueue.main differ in scrolling behaviour (RunLoop-based delivery pauses during scrolling in default mode).

Memory and retain cycles. sink { self.x = $0 } retains self, which retains the cancellable, which retains the closure: a cycle. Use [weak self]. assign(to: \.prop, on: self) also retains self strongly; prefer assign(to: &$prop) (iOS 14+) which ties lifetime to the published property.

Backpressure. Combine has real demand-based backpressure (Subscribers.Demand), unlike AsyncStream producers. sink requests .unlimited, so you normally don't see it; custom subscribers can request .max(n).

Status. Apple has not deprecated Combine, but new APIs (SwiftData, Observation, URLSession async) are async/await based. Verify on any new WWDC.

Real examples. Older Airbnb, Lyft and Instagram-style codebases use Combine or RxSwift; Swift Composable Architecture originally built on Combine and moved to async/await effects; Firebase and Apple frameworks (CoreData fetch publishers, HealthKit) offer publishers.

Analogy. Combine is a factory assembly line with stations (operators), a conveyor (publisher) and a collecting bin (subscriber), and a stop button (cancel).

Common interview traps.

  • Not storing the AnyCancellable.
  • [weak self] forgotten in sink closures causing leaks.
  • Using assign(to:on:self) and creating a retain cycle.
  • Thinking @Published emits the new value inside willSet: subscribers see the old value if they read the property during emission.
  • Believing Combine is dead; it is stable legacy with long life.

notes.title: Combine versus async/await: when each wins
notes.html:
Android equivalent. The question "RxJava or coroutines/Flow?" translates 1:1. Coroutines won on Android for readability and structured concurrency; Swift concurrency is following that path.

Need Winner Why
Single network call, sequential steps async/await Linear code, try, cancellation by Task
Parallel fan-out async let / TaskGroup Structured, cancels children
UI state binding @Observable No subscription code at all
Event stream consumed in one place AsyncStream Simple, cancellation friendly
Search-as-you-type (debounce, switchToLatest) Combine or swift-async-algorithms Operators exist natively
Merge / combineLatest of several sources Combine Mature operators, multicasting
Fan-out to many subscribers Combine subjects Native multicast
Backpressure with demand Combine Real demand model
Libraries/Apple APIs offering publishers Combine at the edge Adapt then convert

Bridging Combine to async.

// Publisher -> AsyncSequence (iOS 15+)
for await value in publisher.values {
    use(value)
}

// Throwing publisher
for try await value in failingPublisher.values { }

// async function -> Publisher (legacy consumers)
func fetchPublisher() -> AnyPublisher<Profile, Error> {
    Future { promise in
        Task {
            do { promise(.success(try await api.fetchProfile())) }
            catch { promise(.failure(error)) }
        }
    }.eraseToAnyPublisher()
}

Debounce in plain async/await (no Combine). A common interview coding task:

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
@MainActor
@Observable
final class SearchModel {
    var query = "" { didSet { scheduleSearch() } }
    private(set) var results: [Item] = []
    private var searchTask: Task<Void, Never>?

    private func scheduleSearch() {
        searchTask?.cancel()
        let q = query
        searchTask = Task {
            try? await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(300))
            guard !Task.isCancelled else { return }
            results = (try? await api.search(q)) ?? []
        }
    }
}
class SearchModel : ViewModel() {
    private var job: Job? = null
    fun onQuery(q: String) {
        job?.cancel()
        job = viewModelScope.launch {
            delay(300)
            results.value = runCatching { api.search(q) }.getOrDefault(emptyList())
        }
    }
}

The cancel-and-replace Task is the simplest debounce and automatically gives switchToLatest semantics because the cancelled Task's Task.sleep throws.

Pitfall of timing logic in async. Task.sleep cancellation throws CancellationError; swallowing with try? then continuing is the bug; check Task.isCancelled after (as above).

Industry stance. New code: async/await + Observation. Apple's own SwiftUI sample code moved away from Combine in 2023 onwards. Existing Combine pipelines are not rewritten for fashion; they are wrapped.

Analogy. async/await is a phone call (one conversation, step by step); Combine is a radio network with relays and filters.

Common interview traps.

  • Declaring one is better universally; the correct answer is by use case and by team codebase.
  • Leaving a Future that wraps a Task: it runs eagerly once at creation, not per subscription (Future is hot and executes immediately).
  • Forgetting .values bridging exists.

notes.title: Observation: @Observable and withObservationTracking
notes.html:
Android equivalent. StateFlow in a ViewModel collected by Compose, or mutableStateOf inside Compose which tracks reads. @Observable is closest to Compose snapshot state: the framework tracks which properties a view's body reads and re-renders only when those change.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
import Observation
import SwiftUI

@MainActor
@Observable
final class CartModel {
    var items: [CartItem] = []
    var coupon: String?
    @ObservationIgnored var analytics: Analytics = .shared   // not tracked

    var total: Decimal { items.reduce(0) { $0 + $1.price } }  // computed, tracks items
}

struct CartView: View {
    @State private var model = CartModel()         // owns it
    var body: some View {
        List(model.items) { Text($0.name) }        // reads items only
        Text(model.total.formatted())              // reads total -> items
    }
}
class CartModel {
    var items by mutableStateOf(listOf<CartItem>())
    var coupon by mutableStateOf<String?>(null)
    val total get() = items.sumOf { it.price }
}

@Composable
fun CartView(model: CartModel = remember { CartModel() }) {
    LazyColumn { items(model.items) { Text(it.name) } }  // reads items only
    Text(model.total.toString())
}

Mechanism. The @Observable macro (Swift 5.9, iOS 17+) rewrites each stored property into a computed property backed by _name, wrapping get with access(keyPath:) and set with withMutation(keyPath:) calls into an ObservationRegistrar. When SwiftUI evaluates body it runs inside withObservationTracking, recording which key paths were read; when any of them mutates, the registrar fires onChange once and SwiftUI schedules a re-evaluation of that view. Contrast with ObservableObject, where objectWillChange fires for any @Published change and invalidates every view observing the object.

withObservationTracking.

func track(_ model: CartModel) {
    withObservationTracking {
        _ = model.items.count                 // apply: reads are recorded
    } onChange: {
        // fires ONCE, just before the change, on the mutating thread
        Task { @MainActor in track(model) }   // re-arm
    }
}

Important: onChange fires once and before the new value is set (willSet semantics), so you must re-arm and read after hopping. That is why you rarely use it by hand; Swift 6.2 / iOS 26 adds an Observations async sequence for this: verify.

Migration table.

Legacy Modern
class VM: ObservableObject @Observable class VM
@Published var x plain var x
@StateObject var vm = VM() @State var vm = VM()
@ObservedObject var vm plain var vm: VM (or let)
@EnvironmentObject @Environment(VM.self)
@Bindable needed to get $vm.x bindings from an @Observable

Gotchas.

  • @Observable works only on classes. Structs are value types and changes propagate through @State.
  • Tracking is per access: reading a property in a non-body context (e.g. in init) tracks nothing.
  • @State private var model = Model() creates a new model each time the parent re-runs its init, though SwiftUI keeps the first instance; the initializer expression may still be evaluated again, so keep model init cheap and do heavy work in .task (a known perf trap, verify on your OS version).
  • Using @Observable types in Task closures: mutations from background threads still fire notifications; keep models @MainActor.
  • Min deployment iOS 17. For iOS 16 and lower you need ObservableObject.

Real examples. Apple's iOS 17 sample apps (Backyard Birds, Food Truck) use @Observable; Point-Free's swift-perception backports Observation to earlier OS versions; Airbnb and Lyft keep ObservableObject where they still support old OS versions.

Analogy. Old way: a school bell rings for all classes whenever anything changes. New way: each teacher (view) gets a message only about the exact student (property) they were watching.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying @Observable uses Combine. It does not.
  • Forgetting @Bindable when you need $model.text with an @Observable passed down as a plain property.
  • Wrapping an @Observable model in @StateObject. Wrong wrapper; use @State.
  • Believing withObservationTracking's onChange fires repeatedly.

notes.title: NotificationCenter, KVO, delegates, target-action
notes.html:
Android equivalent. BroadcastReceiver/LocalBroadcastManager (NotificationCenter), PropertyChangeListener (KVO), listener interfaces (delegates), setOnClickListener (target-action). You must know these: UIKit and Apple frameworks are built on them.

NotificationCenter.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
// Modern: async sequence (iOS 15+)
Task {
    for await _ in NotificationCenter.default.notifications(named: UIApplication.didEnterBackgroundNotification) {
        await flushAnalytics()
    }
}

// Legacy: token-based observer (remember to remove)
let token = NotificationCenter.default.addObserver(
    forName: .NSSystemTimeZoneDidChange, object: nil, queue: .main
) { [weak self] _ in self?.reload() }
// NotificationCenter.default.removeObserver(token)
val receiver = object : BroadcastReceiver() {
    override fun onReceive(c: Context, i: Intent) { reload() }
}
context.registerReceiver(receiver, IntentFilter(Intent.ACTION_TIMEZONE_CHANGED))
// context.unregisterReceiver(receiver)

Notes: Block-based observers return an opaque token you must retain and remove (or they leak); selector-based observers auto-remove on deinit since iOS 9. Posting is synchronous on the poster's thread. In Swift 6, notification payloads (userInfo: [AnyHashable: Any]) are not Sendable, so APIs like notifications(named:) have warnings; verify on your SDK. Define your own names with extension Notification.Name { static let didLogin = Notification.Name("didLogin") }.

KVO (Key-Value Observing). Works on NSObject subclasses with @objc dynamic properties.

final class Player: NSObject {
    @objc dynamic var progress: Double = 0
}

let observation = player.observe(\.progress, options: [.new, .old]) { _, change in
    print(change.newValue ?? 0)
}
// Keep `observation` alive; deallocation of the token stops observing.

The modern block API auto-unregisters when the token deallocs (older addObserver(_:forKeyPath:) crashes with "was deallocated while key value observers were still registered"). KVO is used for AVPlayerItem.status, UIScrollView.contentOffset, WKWebView.estimatedProgress, Operation.isFinished.

Delegates. A protocol plus a weak var delegate. One-to-one, with return values (tableView(_:numberOfRowsInSection:)).

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
protocol UploaderDelegate: AnyObject {
    func uploader(_ u: Uploader, didFinish url: URL)
}
final class Uploader {
    weak var delegate: UploaderDelegate?   // weak to avoid retain cycle
}
interface UploaderListener { fun onFinish(url: Uri) }
class Uploader { var listener: WeakReference<UploaderListener>? = null }

Target-action. button.addTarget(self, action: #selector(tap), for: .touchUpInside); the iOS version of setOnClickListener. iOS 14+ also supports UIAction closures: UIButton(primaryAction: UIAction { _ in ... }).

Mechanism Cardinality Typical use
NotificationCenter many-to-many App lifecycle, keyboard, locale
KVO many observers of one property Apple framework properties
Delegate one-to-one with return value UIKit data sources, CLLocationManager
Target-action one control to one target UIKit controls
Closure one-to-one Completion handlers

Production incidents. KVO crash signature: NSInternalInconsistencyException: An instance ... was deallocated while key value observers were still registered with it. Leaked block-based NotificationCenter observers that retain self. Delegate declared strong causing view controller leaks, seen in the Memory Graph Debugger as a cycle.

Analogy. NotificationCenter is a town loudspeaker; KVO is a motion sensor on a particular door; a delegate is a personal assistant you phone with questions; target-action is a doorbell wired to one room.

Common interview traps.

  • Strong delegate references (must be weak, protocol constrained to AnyObject).
  • Forgetting to retain/remove the NotificationCenter token.
  • Using KVO on a pure Swift class without NSObject and @objc dynamic.
  • Android mix-up: NotificationCenter is in-process only; it is not a system-wide broadcast like Android intents.

notes.title: Recipes: debounce, throttle, combineLatest, merge
notes.html:
Android equivalent. The Flow operators debounce, sample, combine, merge. In Swift, pick Combine (existing code) or swift-async-algorithms (new code; Apple package added via SPM).

swift-async-algorithms.

import AsyncAlgorithms

// debounce
for await text in queryStream.debounce(for: .milliseconds(300)) {
    await search(text)
}

// throttle: at most one per interval
for await pos in scrollStream._throttle(for: .milliseconds(100)) { }   // verify name; was `_throttle` in some releases

// merge two streams of the same element type
for await e in merge(localEvents, remoteEvents) { }

// combineLatest
for await (user, prefs) in combineLatest(userStream, prefsStream) { }

Same recipes in Combine.

Publishers.CombineLatest($email, $password)
    .map { !$0.isEmpty && $1.count >= 8 }
    .assign(to: &$canSubmit)

$a.merge(with: $b)
$scroll.throttle(for: .milliseconds(100), scheduler: DispatchQueue.main, latest: true)
Recipe Combine Async
debounce .debounce(for:scheduler:) AsyncAlgorithms.debounce or cancel-and-replace Task
throttle .throttle(for:scheduler:latest:) AsyncAlgorithms throttle (verify)
combineLatest CombineLatest combineLatest
merge merge(with:) merge
retry .retry(n) loop with try and Task.sleep
timeout .timeout(...) withThrowingTaskGroup racing a sleep

Manual timeout recipe.

func withTimeout<T: Sendable>(_ seconds: Double, _ op: @escaping @Sendable () async throws -> T) async throws -> T {
    try await withThrowingTaskGroup(of: T.self) { group in
        group.addTask { try await op() }
        group.addTask {
            try await Task.sleep(for: .seconds(seconds))
            throw CancellationError()       // use a TimeoutError in real code
        }
        defer { group.cancelAll() }
        return try await group.next()!
    }
}

SwiftUI shortcut. .task(id: query) { try? await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(300)); await model.search(query) } is an idiomatic debounce: when id changes, SwiftUI cancels the old task and starts a new one (the sleep throws on cancel and the search is skipped).

Real examples. Search boxes in Airbnb/Spotify-style apps, form validation (combineLatest), scroll tracking (throttle), merging push and polling updates.

Analogy. Debounce waits for someone to finish talking before replying; throttle answers once per minute no matter how often asked; combineLatest is a dashboard that updates when either gauge moves.

Common interview traps.

  • Using throttle when you need debounce (search box) or vice versa.
  • Forgetting the scheduler argument in Combine, so updates arrive off main.
  • Trusting operator names without checking the swift-async-algorithms version; mark verify.

notes.title: Backpressure and memory pitfalls
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Flow has built-in suspension backpressure (emit suspends) and buffer/conflate. In Swift, AsyncSequence consumers pull (next()), but AsyncStream producers push into a buffer, and Combine subjects push to subscribers; backpressure depends on the source.

Where memory goes wrong.

  1. Unbounded AsyncStream buffer on a hot source with a slow consumer. Set .bufferingNewest(n).
  2. Combine PassthroughSubject pushing faster than a sink that does heavy synchronous work on its scheduler; use buffer, throttle, or receive(on:) with care.
  3. Retain cycles: sink/Task/NotificationCenter block capturing self strongly while self stores the cancellable/task.
  4. Unfinished streams: producers that never call finish(), onTermination forgotten, so the system resource (CLLocationManager, Bluetooth) stays active, draining battery. The battery shows up in Xcode's Energy gauge and Organizer's energy metrics.
  5. Multiple for await loops started repeatedly (for example in onAppear without cancellation) leading to N parallel consumers. Use .task { }, which is cancelled on disappear.
  6. Unstructured Task stored in a view model without cancellation in deinit.
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
@MainActor
@Observable
final class LiveModel {
    private(set) var latest: Reading?
    private var listenTask: Task<Void, Never>?

    func start(_ stream: AsyncStream<Reading>) {
        listenTask?.cancel()
        listenTask = Task { [weak self] in
            for await r in stream {
                guard let self else { return }
                self.latest = r
            }
        }
    }
    func stop() { listenTask?.cancel() }
    isolated deinit { listenTask?.cancel() }   // Swift 6.2; verify, else cancel in stop()/onDisappear
}
class LiveModel : ViewModel() {
    val latest = MutableStateFlow<Reading?>(null)
    private var job: Job? = null
    fun start(flow: Flow<Reading>) {
        job?.cancel()
        job = viewModelScope.launch { flow.collect { latest.value = it } }
    }
}

Diagnosing. Instruments: Allocations (growth over time and generation marks), Leaks, and the Swift Concurrency template (Tasks that never end). Xcode Memory Graph Debugger shows cycles between a view model, a Task and a cancellable. MetricKit memory metrics and Jetsam (EXC_RESOURCE, "terminated due to memory pressure") appear in Organizer.

Design guidance.

  • Pick buffering by data semantics: state (newest wins), events (must not drop: bounded buffer and slow-consumer strategy), metrics (drop).
  • Always pair resource acquisition with onTermination/awaitClose.
  • Prefer one long-lived consumer with explicit lifecycle over many ad hoc ones.
  • Convert high-frequency raw data to sampled or windowed data before it reaches the UI.

Analogy. A kitchen window: if cooks (producers) fill it faster than the waiter (consumer) carries plates, plates pile up and eventually collapse the window unless you pick which to throw away.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing AsyncStream provides Kotlin-style suspension of the producer.
  • Leaving Task { for await ... } in init with strong self, never cancelled.
  • Claiming Combine has no backpressure (it has demand), or that sink uses it (it requests unlimited).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Modern stack: AsyncSequence/AsyncStream for event streams, @Observable for UI state; Combine and ObservableObject are stable legacy you must read fluently.
  • AsyncStream is the iOS callbackFlow: yield from callbacks, release resources in onTermination, pick a buffering policy (unbounded, bufferingNewest, bufferingOldest).
  • Streams are typically single-consumer and have no built-in debounce/merge/combineLatest; use swift-async-algorithms, Combine, or a cancel-and-replace Task / .task(id:).
  • Combine: publishers, subscribers, subjects, AnyCancellable must be stored, [weak self] in sinks, .values bridges to async.
  • @Observable tracks property reads per view and re-renders precisely; migrate @StateObject to @State, @ObservedObject to a plain property, use @Bindable for bindings.
  • withObservationTracking fires once, before the change; re-arm manually, or use the newer Observations sequence (verify).
  • Old toolbox: NotificationCenter (retain/remove tokens), KVO (NSObject, @objc dynamic), delegates (weak), target-action.
  • Memory: bound buffers, always terminate producers, cancel stored Tasks, watch retain cycles via the Memory Graph and Instruments.
